Short Stories: Twists, Secrets and Revenge

Maupassant, O. Henry, Saki and Poe · Anglais · Première et Terminale (lycée général et technologique), bac pro · Six lessons

1. Axe du programme

Programme d’anglais du lycée général et technologique, BO n° 22 du 29 mai 2025, en vigueur en Première et en Terminale depuis la rentrée 2026.

ClasseAxe principalAxes possibles aussi
PremièreAxe 1. Identités et échanges. Une nouvelle française étudiée en cours de français relue en anglais (lesson 3) : ce que la traduction garde, perd et gagne ; quatre auteurs, deux langues, trois pays.Axe 2. Diversité et inclusion : la place sociale et les apparences, de la femme du petit commis chez Maupassant au jeune couple pauvre de New York chez O. Henry.
TerminaleAxe 3. Fictions et réalités. La nouvelle comme machine à surprendre : la chute, l’ironie, le narrateur auquel on ne peut pas se fier (Poe), et ce que la fiction dit du réel (l’orgueil, la pauvreté, la haine héritée).Axe 1. Espace privé et espace public : les secrets du couple (les Loisel cachent la perte, Della et Jim leurs sacrifices). Axe 2. Territoire et mémoire : une querelle de terre sur trois générations (Saki), un crime gardé cinquante ans dans les catacombes d’une famille (Poe).
LLCER anglaisPremière : thématique « Rencontres », axe « L’amour et l’amitié » (The Gift of the Magi, The Interlopers).Première : thématique « Imaginaires », axe « Imaginaires effrayants » (Poe). Terminale : thématique « Expression et construction de soi », axe « Mise en scène de soi » (Mathilde et les apparences, Montresor narrateur).
Bac proLe programme de langues vivantes de la voie professionnelle (BO spécial n° 5 du 11 avril 2019) n’impose pas d’axe : la séquence en travaille la dimension culturelle (deux nouvelles du monde anglophone et une nouvelle française en traduction) et prépare l’oral de l’examen (prise de parole en continu à partir d’un document, puis échange).Lien direct avec le programme de français de la voie professionnelle : La Parure y est étudiée (Première bac pro, semaines 10 et 11).

2. Problématique

How do short stories surprise us, and what do their twists reveal about pride, love and revenge? Comment les nouvelles nous surprennent-elles, et que révèlent leurs chutes de l’orgueil, de l’amour et de la vengeance ?

Lesson 1: How is a short story built, from its first line to its last surprise? · Lesson 2: Why does a borrowed necklace cost Mathilde ten years of her life? · Lesson 3: What does a translation keep, lose and gain? · Lesson 4: Why does the narrator call Della and Jim “the wisest”? · Lesson 5: Who are the real interlopers in the forest? · Lesson 6: Can we trust Montresor, the narrator of “The Cask of Amontillado”?

3. Objectifs linguistiques

  • Telling a plot: one day, suddenly, then, at that moment, finally; the present simple to sum up (lesson 1).
  • The past simple and the past perfect: she lost the necklace that she had borrowed (lesson 2).
  • Comparing two texts: both, whereas, unlike, the same as, shorter than (lesson 3).
  • The second conditional: If I were Della, I would … (lesson 4).
  • The past continuous and the past simple: he was patrolling the forest when he met Georg (lesson 5).
  • Modals of deduction about the past: he must have planned it, he may have felt guilty (lesson 6).
  • Language activities : compréhension de l’écrit (quatre nouvelles intégrales, un texte et sa traduction), expression orale en continu (raconter une fin, présenter une œuvre), interaction orale (jeu de rôle, débat, hot seat), expression écrite (journal, dialogue, nouvelle fin, nouvelle à chute).

4. Ancrage culturel

La nouvelle à chute : Guy de Maupassant, La Parure (1884) et sa traduction anglaise ; O. Henry, The Gift of the Magi (New York, 1905) ; Saki, The Interlopers (1919) ; Edgar Allan Poe, The Cask of Amontillado (1846) et la théorie de l’« effet unique » (compte rendu de Hawthorne, 1842). La littérature comparée : un texte, deux langues. Œuvres : Vallotton, Tissot, Hassam, Shishkin, Harry Clarke.

5. Niveau CECRL

  • Première : B1+ vers B2.
  • Terminale LV1 : B2 vers C1, avec un parcours C1/C2 à la fin de chaque lesson.
  • Bac pro (Version B) : B1, version allégée en trois lessons (The Necklace, la littérature comparée, The Gift of the Magi).
  • Dys-friendly version : B1, les six lessons, une étape à la fois.

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 1: How a short story works

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: The opening lines of the four stories of the sequence, with the story arc and the types of hook and ending

  • “The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could, but when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge.” (Poe, The Cask of Amontillado, 1846)
  • “One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all.” (O. Henry, The Gift of the Magi, 1905)
  • “The girl was one of those pretty and charming young creatures who sometimes are born, as if by a slip of fate, into a family of clerks.” (Maupassant, The Necklace, 1884, transl. Project Gutenberg #3090)
  • “A short story can be read in one sitting. Edgar Allan Poe, one of the inventors of the genre, wanted every word to serve a single effect.” (Lesson document)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticePoeWhat strikes you first?
“A short story can be read in one sitting”; Poe “wanted every word to serve a single effect” (lesson document).
Few characters, one main event: everything in a short story leads to one effect, very often a final surprise.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesOpeningsWhich clues? In which line?
“One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all.” (O. Henry); “I vowed revenge.” (Poe); “as if by a slip of fate, into a family of clerks” (Maupassant).
A precise detail, a shocking statement and a portrait: each first line raises a question that the reader wants answered.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandArcWhat effect? What contrast?
Exposition, inciting incident, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution (story arc table).
Tension grows up to a turning point; in our four stories, the resolution hides a twist.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictEndingsWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: every short story ends with a happy surprise.
Not confirmed: a twist can be bitter (situational irony in The Necklace), tender (The Gift of the Magi) or terrible (“Wolves.” in The Interlopers); an ending can also be open or moral (endings table).
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningAllWhich interpretation do I defend?
“when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge” (Poe) and “That was all.” (O. Henry).
A short story is built from its last line backwards: a hook to catch us, rising tension, and a twist that makes us reread the story differently.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in the story (or in the translation). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 1: How a short story works · Dys-friendly version

Question: How is a short story built, from its first line to its last surprise?

Four words:

  • exposition: the beginning: who, where, when
  • inciting incident: the event that starts the problem
  • rising action: the part where tension grows
  • climax: the turning point of the story

One line to read: “The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could, but when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge.” (Poe, The Cask of Amontillado, 1846)

Steps: 1. Read the line aloud. 2. Learn the four words. 3. Do the spiral below, one step at a time. 4. Say your answer with the support sentence.

Objective

Understand how a short story is built, from its first line to its last surprise. Final task of the sequence: write the opening and the twist of your own short story.

What is a short story?

A short story can be read in one sitting. Edgar Allan Poe, one of the inventors of the genre, wanted every word to serve a single effect. Few characters, one main event, and very often a final surprise.

1. The story arc

StageQuestion to askKey words
ExpositionWho? Where? When?setting, characters
Inciting incidentWhat starts the problem?suddenly, one day
Rising actionHow does tension grow?then, as, while
ClimaxWhat is the turning point?at that moment
Falling actionWhat are the consequences?after that
ResolutionHow does it end?finally, in the end

2. Hooking the reader

Type of hookHow it worksOur stories
In medias resthe story starts in the middle of the actionThe Interlopers
A shocking statementthe narrator confesses something strongThe Cask of Amontillado
A precise detaila number or object raises a questionThe Gift of the Magi
A portraita character and her desireThe Necklace

Worksheet: match each opening with a type of hook

Opening lineType of hook
“The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could, but when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge.”...
“One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all.”...
“The girl was one of those pretty and charming young creatures who sometimes are born, as if by a slip of fate, into a family of clerks.”...
Answer key
  • The Cask of Amontillado: A shocking statement
  • The Gift of the Magi: A precise detail
  • The Necklace: A portrait

3. Twist endings

Type of endingDefinitionEffect on the reader
Twist endingan unexpected final revelationsurprise, we reread the story differently
Situational ironythe result is the opposite of what the characters expectbitterness or tenderness
Open endingthe reader must imagine what comes nextsuspense, discussion
Moral endingthe narrator gives a lessonreflection

Speaking

In pairs, tell the ending of a film or series that surprised you. Your partner names the type of ending.

Writing

Write the first sentence of a story using one type of hook (one or two sentences).

Homework · required

To do for next lesson. It is checked at the start of the lesson in the Recap check.

  1. Exercise 1 · Put the stages of the arc in order: climax, exposition, resolution, rising action, inciting incident, falling action.
  2. Exercise 2 · Match: (a) In medias res (b) A shocking statement (c) A precise detail. 1. “One dollar and eighty-seven cents.” 2. The story starts in the middle of the action. 3. “I vowed revenge.”
  3. Exercise 3 · Write the first two sentences of a story with a hook (30 words).
Answer key: homework
  1. exposition, inciting incident, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution
  2. a2, b3, c1
  3. Model: “The letter had been waiting under the door for ten years. Nobody in the house dared to open it.”

For the teacher

Gerex stepWhat the class does
Warm up (5 min)Recall of the last story in three sentences, cold calling or volunteers.
Discovery (15 min)Reading of the text or extract of the opening lines, first with a gist question.
Analysis (20 min)Tables in pairs, text dependent questions, shared correction.
Speaking (10 min)Short oral task, the teacher circulates and notes two strengths per group.
Writing (5 min + homework)Short writing task, finished at home.
NeedLever
Struggling readersGlossary given in advance, audio reading by the teacher, questions 1 to 3 only.
Fast finishersExtension question, a quotation to explain, a sentence of the story to translate into French.
Dys studentsDys version of the page: Lexend font, larger spacing, sentence starters, shorter tasks.
Recap check, how to run itDetail
Before the bellThe questions are on the board or projected when students walk in.
Minutes 0 to 4Everyone writes; no talking. The teacher takes the register meanwhile.
Minute 4Random draw of three names (cards, app or dice), oral answers.
MarkingMarks on the scale given, noted in the gradebook; homework checked at the same time.
WhyNot one idle minute: the class starts the moment students enter, and homework is reinforced.

If a student cannot attend class or is in hospital

Lesson 1: How a short story works. Your lesson at home or in hospital, about 40 minutes, at your own pace. Stop when you are tired: you can do it in two parts.

  1. Read the key lines aloud, slowly, twice:
    • “The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could, but when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge.” (Poe, The Cask of Amontillado, 1846)
    • “One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all.” (O. Henry, The Gift of the Magi, 1905)
    • “The girl was one of those pretty and charming young creatures who sometimes are born, as if by a slip of fate, into a family of clerks.” (Maupassant, The Necklace, 1884, transl. Project Gutenberg #3090)
    • “A short story can be read in one sitting. Edgar Allan Poe, one of the inventors of the genre, wanted every word to serve a single effect.” (Lesson document)
  2. Learn the eight words of the Vocabulary box of the lesson: exposition, inciting incident, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution, hook, twist.
  3. Do the spirale de Gorse: copy the five steps on your worksheet (or use the worksheet of this lesson). For each step, write one idea and one line from the text. Then check below.
  4. Quick check: Complete with: exposition, inciting incident, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution, hook, twist.
    • The ______ tells us who, where and when.
    • The invitation to a ball is the ______ of The Necklace.
    • During the ______, tension grows.
    • The ______ is the turning point.
    • The ______ shows the consequences.
    • The ______ is how the story ends.
    • A good ______ catches the reader in the first line.
    • A ______ makes us reread the whole story.
  5. Send to your teacher through the school’s online messaging: copy the six steps of the story arc. Then tell the plot of a film or series you know in six sentences, one per step, with one, suddenly, then, at that moment, after that, finally.

A precise detail, a shocking statement and a portrait: each first line raises a question that the reader wants answered.

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 2: The Necklace

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Guy de Maupassant, “The Necklace” (La Parure, 1884), English translation, Project Gutenberg #3090

  • “She had no gowns, no jewels, nothing. And she loved nothing but that. She felt made for that.” (The Necklace, opening)
  • “This life lasted ten years.” (The Necklace)
  • “She had become the woman of impoverished households, strong and hard and rough.” (The Necklace)
  • ““Oh, my poor Mathilde! Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!”” (The Necklace, last line)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeOpeningWhat strikes you first?
“She had no gowns, no jewels, nothing. And she loved nothing but that. She felt made for that.”
The negations and “made for that” show the gap between her dream and her real life as the wife of a clerk.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesThe lossWhich clues? In which line?
To replace the lost necklace, Loisel goes “laying upon the jeweler's counter thirty-six thousand francs.”
Instead of telling the truth, the couple buys a copy: pride turns a loss into a huge debt.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandTen yearsWhat effect? What contrast?
“This life lasted ten years.” and “strong and hard and rough”.
One short sentence alone in its paragraph sums up ten years; the repeated “and” shows the weight of the work.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictLast lineWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: the sacrifice was useful, because the Loisels replaced a real diamond necklace.
Not confirmed: “Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!” The twist turns ten years of work into bitter irony.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningNarratorWhich interpretation do I defend?
“How strange and changeful is life! How small a thing is needed to make or ruin us!”
A small thing ruins her, but pride and appearances are responsible too: she borrowed to look rich and never dared to tell the truth.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in the story (or in the translation). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 2: The Necklace · Dys-friendly version

Question: Why does a borrowed necklace cost Mathilde ten years of her life?

Four words:

  • dowry: money a bride brings to her marriage
  • clerk: an office worker in a ministry
  • to borrow: to take something you will give back
  • ball: an elegant evening party with dancing

One line to read: “She had no gowns, no jewels, nothing. And she loved nothing but that. She felt made for that.” (The Necklace, opening)

Steps: 1. Read the line aloud. 2. Learn the four words. 3. Do the spiral below, one step at a time. 4. Say your answer with the support sentence.

  • “This life lasted ten years.” (The Necklace)
  • “She had become the woman of impoverished households, strong and hard and rough.” (The Necklace)
  • ““Oh, my poor Mathilde! Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!”” (The Necklace, last line)

The story

Paris, the 1880s. Mathilde Loisel, married to a modest clerk, dreams of luxury. An invitation to a ball and a borrowed necklace change her life for ten long years.

Read the full text of The Necklace (public domain)

From La Parure to The Necklace

You already know this story from French class. In the next lesson, Comparative literature, you will put the French and English texts side by side.

Describe and interpret the picture

Look at the illustration at the top of the page. You can see: a young woman in a pink ball gown, a fan, men in black evening dress, a crowded salon, chandeliers.

  1. Describe the picture in three sentences.
  2. Which moment of the story could it show? What does her face suggest about her desire to be admired?
  3. Find one sentence of the text that matches the picture.

Useful phrases: It shows… · In the foreground / background… · The colours suggest… · This reminds me of the moment when… · It reveals that… · I think the artist wants us to feel…

Answer key

The ball at the Ministry: Mathilde is the prettiest woman there and every man looks at her. Her triumph is the life she believes she deserves.

“She had no gowns, no jewels, nothing. And she loved nothing but that. She felt made for that.”
Maupassant, “The Diamond Necklace”, transl. Project Gutenberg #3090

1. Vocabulary

WordMeaningEn français
dowrymoney a bride brings to her marriagedot
clerkan office worker in a ministrycommis, employé
to borrowto take something you will give backemprunter
ballan elegant evening party with dancingbal
jewela precious stone or ornamentbijou
to replaceto put a new thing instead of a lost oneremplacer
debtmoney you owedette
to sacrificeto give up something precioussacrifier
pridea strong sense of your own dignityfierté, orgueil
pasteimitation stones made of glassstrass, faux

2. Characters

CharacterWho?WantsWhat happens
Mathilde Loiselyoung wife of a clerkluxury, admirationten years of hard work, poverty
Monsieur Loiselher husband, a modest clerkto make her happysacrifices his savings and his youth
Madame Forestiera rich school friendto help Mathildelearns the truth at the end

3. The arc of the story

StageIn this story
ExpositionMathilde is unhappy with her modest life.
Inciting incidentThe invitation to the Minister's ball.
Rising actionThe dress, the borrowed necklace, the triumph at the ball.
ClimaxThe necklace is lost.
Falling actionTen years of debt and work.
Resolution and twistThe necklace was paste, worth five hundred francs.

4. Text dependent questions

  1. Why is Mathilde unhappy at the start of the story?
  2. How does her husband react to her tears about the dress?
  3. What does Mathilde choose at Madame Forestier's, and why?
  4. What do the Loisels decide when the necklace is lost?
  5. How does Mathilde change during the ten years?
  6. Explain the twist ending.
Answer key
  1. She feels born for luxury but lives in a modest home with a clerk; she suffers from the gap between her dreams and her reality.
  2. He gives her the four hundred francs he saved for a gun, which shows his love and his sacrifice.
  3. A diamond necklace: it is the most dazzling jewel, it matches her dream of elegance.
  4. They buy a similar necklace for thirty six thousand francs and return it without telling the truth.
  5. She becomes strong, rough and poor; she does the heavy housework and bargains at the market.
  6. Madame Forestier reveals that the necklace was imitation, worth at most five hundred francs: ten years were sacrificed for nothing.

5. Speaking

Role play in pairs: Mathilde meets Madame Forestier ten years later. One student is Mathilde, the other her friend. Two minutes, then switch.

6. Writing

Write Mathilde's diary entry on the night of the ball (80 to 120 words). Use the past simple and at least four words from the vocabulary table.

Homework · required

To do for next lesson. It is checked at the start of the lesson in the Recap check.

  1. Exercise 1 · Gap-fill: Mathilde …… a necklace from her friend. She …… it after the ball. The Loisels pay their …… for ten years. In the end, the necklace was …… . (borrows, loses, debt, paste)
  2. Exercise 2 · True or false? Justify. a) Monsieur Loisel is rich. b) Mathilde chooses a diamond necklace. c) Madame Forestier knows the truth at the start.
  3. Exercise 3 · Answer in 50 words: is Mathilde a victim or responsible for her fate?
Answer key: homework
  1. borrows · loses · debt · paste
  2. a) False, he is a modest clerk. b) True. c) False, she learns at the end that they replaced it.
  3. Model: Mathilde is partly a victim of her social class, but her pride is responsible: she borrows a jewel to appear rich and never dares to tell the truth, which costs her ten years.

If a student cannot attend class or is in hospital

Lesson 2: The Necklace. Your lesson at home or in hospital, about 40 minutes, at your own pace. Stop when you are tired: you can do it in two parts.

  1. Read the key lines aloud, slowly, twice:
    • “She had no gowns, no jewels, nothing. And she loved nothing but that. She felt made for that.” (The Necklace, opening)
    • “This life lasted ten years.” (The Necklace)
    • “She had become the woman of impoverished households, strong and hard and rough.” (The Necklace)
    • ““Oh, my poor Mathilde! Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!”” (The Necklace, last line)
  2. Learn the eight words of the Vocabulary box of the lesson: dowry, clerk, to borrow, ball, jewel, debt, pride, paste.
  3. Do the spirale de Gorse: copy the five steps on your worksheet (or use the worksheet of this lesson). For each step, write one idea and one line from the text. Then check below.
  4. Quick check: Complete with: dowry, clerk, borrow, ball, jewel, debt, pride, paste.
    • Mathilde had no ______, so she could not marry a rich man.
    • Her husband is a modest ______.
    • She decides to ______ a necklace from her friend.
    • They are invited to a ______ at the Ministry.
    • A diamond is a precious ______.
    • The Loisels pay their ______ for ten years.
    • Her ______ stops her from telling the truth.
    • In the end, the necklace was ______.
  5. Send to your teacher through the school’s online messaging: read the opening and the end of the story. Write Mathilde’s diary entry on the night of the ball (100 words) with two verbs in the past perfect.
Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (Opening): “She had no gowns, no jewels, nothing. And she loved nothing but that. She felt made for that.” The negations and “made for that” show the gap between her dream and her real life as the wife of a clerk.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (The loss): To replace the lost necklace, Loisel goes “laying upon the jeweler's counter thirty-six thousand francs.” Instead of telling the truth, the couple buys a copy: pride turns a loss into a huge debt.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Ten years): “This life lasted ten years.” and “strong and hard and rough”. One short sentence alone in its paragraph sums up ten years; the repeated “and” shows the weight of the work.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (Last line): Hypothesis: the sacrifice was useful, because the Loisels replaced a real diamond necklace. Not confirmed: “Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!” The twist turns ten years of work into bitter irony.
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (Narrator): “How strange and changeful is life! How small a thing is needed to make or ruin us!” A small thing ruins her, but pride and appearances are responsible too: she borrowed to look rich and never dared to tell the truth.
Check my quick check
  1. dowry
  2. clerk
  3. borrow
  4. ball
  5. jewel
  6. debt
  7. pride
  8. paste

If something is difficult, write your question at the end of your work: your teacher will answer it.

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 3: Comparative literature: La Parure and The Necklace

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Guy de Maupassant, « La Parure » (Contes du jour et de la nuit, 1885, Wikisource) and its English translation (Project Gutenberg #3090), side by side

  • “« C’était une de ces jolies et charmantes filles, nées, comme par une erreur du destin, dans une famille d’employés. » / “as if by a slip of fate, into a family of clerks.”” (La Parure / The Necklace, opening)
  • “« Elle n’avait pas de toilettes, pas de bijoux, rien. » / “She had no gowns, no jewels, nothing.”” (La Parure / The Necklace)
  • “« Et cette vie dura dix ans. » / “This life lasted ten years.”” (La Parure / The Necklace)
  • “« Mais la mienne était fausse. Elle valait au plus cinq cents francs !… » / “Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!”” (La Parure / The Necklace, last line)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeOpeningWhat strikes you first?
« comme par une erreur du destin » becomes “as if by a slip of fate”.
“Slip” is lighter than « erreur »: fate looks accidental, and the narrator’s irony is kept.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesWordsWhich clues? In which line?
« Elle n’avait pas de toilettes » becomes “She had no gowns”.
« toilettes » is a false friend: the translator chooses “gowns”, elegant dresses, not toilets.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandRhythmWhat effect? What contrast?
« Et cette vie dura dix ans. » (6 words) / “This life lasted ten years.” (5 words), each alone in its paragraph.
The rhythm is kept: one short sentence stops the reader and sums up ten years.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictLast lineWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: the twist is exactly the same in English.
Partly confirmed: “paste” keeps the surprise, but « fausse » is clearer, and « !… » leaves a silence that the English “!” loses. The double meaning of « La Parure » (a set of jewels, and finery) is lost in the title.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
“as if by a slip of fate” and “Why, my necklace was paste!”
A translation keeps the story, the irony and the rhythm, but it loses sounds and double meanings: reading both texts shows the choices behind every word.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in the story (or in the translation). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 3: Comparative literature: La Parure and The Necklace · Dys-friendly version

Question: What does a translation keep, lose and gain?

Four words:

  • original: the text as the author wrote it
  • translation: the text rewritten in another language
  • translator: the person who translates
  • false friend: a word that looks the same but means something else

One line to read: “« C’était une de ces jolies et charmantes filles, nées, comme par une erreur du destin, dans une famille d’employés. »” (La Parure / The Necklace, opening)

Steps: 1. Read the line aloud. 2. Learn the four words. 3. Do the spiral below, one step at a time. 4. Say your answer with the support sentence.

Introduction to comparative literature

Comparative literature studies texts across languages and cultures. Here we compare a text with its translation: the same story, two languages. What is kept? What is lost? What is gained?

You studied La Parure in French class. Today the same extracts come back, side by side with the English translation.

1. Key notions

NotionDefinition
Originalthe text as the author wrote it, here Maupassant's French (1884)
Translationthe text rewritten in another language, here English (Project Gutenberg)
Translator's choiceeach word the translator selects among several possibilities
Loss and gaina meaning, a sound or a rhythm that disappears, or a new effect that appears
Cultural referencea detail that belongs to one culture: francs, the Ministry, a dowry
Rhythmthe length of sentences and paragraphs, punctuation, repetition
Twist in both languagesdoes the final surprise strike as hard in English?

2. Side by side

Maupassant (French original)English translationFrench course reference
« C’était une de ces jolies et charmantes filles, nées, comme par une erreur du destin, dans une famille d’employés. »The girl was one of those pretty and charming young creatures who sometimes are born, as if by a slip of fate, into a family of clerks.Français 2de, séquence « Le roman : personnages et intrigues », séance 2 « L'intrigue et la chute : La Parure » ; Bac pro 1re français, semaine 10, leçon 1 « La Parure : la situation initiale »
« Elle n’avait pas de dot, pas d’espérances, aucun moyen d’être connue, comprise, aimée, épousée par un homme riche et distingué ; et elle se laissa marier avec un petit commis du ministère de l’instruction publique. »She had no dowry, no expectations, no way of being known, understood, loved, married by any rich and distinguished man; so she let herself be married to a little clerk of the Ministry of Public Instruction.Bac pro 1re français, semaine 10, leçon 1 « La Parure : la situation initiale »
« Elle n’avait pas de toilettes, pas de bijoux, rien. Et elle n’aimait que cela ; elle se sentait faite pour cela. »She had no gowns, no jewels, nothing. And she loved nothing but that. She felt made for that.Français 2de, séquence « Le roman : personnages et intrigues », séance 2 « L'intrigue et la chute : La Parure »
« Et cette vie dura dix ans. »This life lasted ten years.LettresPro, méthode « Lire le rythme d'un texte »
« Elle était devenue la femme forte, et dure, et rude, des ménages pauvres. »She had become the woman of impoverished households, strong and hard and rough.LettresPro, méthode « Lire le rythme d'un texte »
« Comme la vie est singulière, changeante ! »How strange and changeful is life!LettresPro, méthode « Lire le rythme d'un texte »
« Et elle souriait d’une joie orgueilleuse et naïve. »And she smiled with a joy that was at once proud and ingenuous.Français 2de, séquence « Le roman : personnages et intrigues », séance 2 « L'intrigue et la chute : La Parure »
« Oh ! ma pauvre Mathilde ! Mais la mienne était fausse. Elle valait au plus cinq cents francs !… »“Oh, my poor Mathilde! Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!”Français 2de, séquence « Le roman : personnages et intrigues », séance 2 « L'intrigue et la chute : La Parure » ; LettresPro, méthode « Lire le rythme d'un texte »

French text: Guy de Maupassant, « La Parure », Contes du jour et de la nuit, C. Marpon et E. Flammarion, 1885, p. 73 to 93, Wikisource, link. English text: Project Gutenberg eBook #3090, link. The dialogue dash of the French and a long dash of the English are not shown.

3. Word choices

FrenchEnglishComment
erreur du destinslip of fate“error” becomes “slip”: lighter, almost accidental
commisclerksocial rank kept; « petit » becomes “little”
dotdowryexact equivalent, a cultural reference to marriage customs
toilettesgownsfalse friend avoided: elegant dresses, not bathrooms
naïveingenuousa learned word chosen instead of “naive”
faussepastetechnical word for imitation jewels: the reader must know it
singulière, changeantestrange and changefultwo adjectives kept, order of the sentence inverted
La ParureThe Diamond Necklace / The Necklace« parure » also means finery, adornment: the double meaning is lost

4. False friends

French wordLooks likeMeans
toilettestoiletselegant dresses, gowns
naïvenaive (exists, but)the translator prefers “ingenuous”
dotdot (a small point)dowry
commiscommitteda junior clerk
misèremisery (sadness)extreme poverty

5. Rhythm and punctuation

Remember the LettresPro method: a short sentence stops the reader, a long one slows him down.

FrenchEnglishKept or changed?
« Et cette vie dura dix ans. » 6 words, a paragraph alone“This life lasted ten years.” 5 words, a paragraph alonekept: ten years in one short sentence
« forte, et dure, et rude » : et repeated“strong and hard and rough”: and repeatedkept: the heavy repetition shows the weight of work
« rien. Et elle n’aimait que cela ; elle se sentait » : one sentence with a semicolon“nothing. And she loved nothing but that. She felt…”: two sentenceschanged: the English is more abrupt
« !… » at the end: exclamation and suspension“!” onlypartly lost: the French leaves a silence after the twist

6. Cultural references and tone

In FrenchIn EnglishEffect
francsfrancs keptthe reader stays in Paris
ministère de l’instruction publiqueMinistry of Public Instructionliteral; today we say Ministry of Education
louislouis keptold gold coins, an unknown word for English readers
Mme Loisel, Mme ForestierMadame Loisel, Madame ForestierFrench titles kept, foreign flavour

Tone. The ironic narrator of Maupassant stays ironic in English: “a slip of fate”, “proud and ingenuous”. The twist keeps its force, but the final « !… » loses its silence.

Guided comparison

  1. Compare the first sentences: which word replaces « erreur »? Is the effect the same?
  2. Why does the translator write “gowns” and not “toilets”?
  3. Count the words of « Et cette vie dura dix ans. » and of its translation. Is the rhythm kept?
  4. Is the twist as strong in English? Justify with the last line.
Answer key
  1. “slip”: the English makes fate look accidental, less tragic.
  2. « toilettes » is a false friend: here it means elegant dresses.
  3. 6 and 5 words, both alone in a paragraph: the rhythm is kept.
  4. Yes, “paste” is the key word, but « fausse » is clearer and « !… » adds a silence that the English loses.

Comparative writing

Write a comparative paragraph of 120 to 150 words: does the English translation keep the irony and the twist of La Parure? Use two quotations, one in each language.
Answer key (model)

The translation keeps the ironic voice of the narrator: “as if by a slip of fate” echoes « comme par une erreur du destin ». It also keeps the short paragraph “This life lasted ten years.” But it loses the double meaning of the title, since « parure » means both a set of jewels and finery, and the final « !… » becomes a simple exclamation: the silence after the twist disappears.

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 4: The Gift of the Magi

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: O. Henry, “The Gift of the Magi” (1905), in The Four Million, Project Gutenberg #7256

  • “One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all.” (The Gift of the Magi, opening)
  • “One was Jim’s gold watch that had been his father’s and his grandfather’s. The other was Della’s hair.” (The Gift of the Magi)
  • “I sold the watch to get the money to buy your combs.” (The Gift of the Magi, Jim)
  • “of all who give gifts these two were the wisest.” (The Gift of the Magi, last paragraph)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeOpeningWhat strikes you first?
“One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all.”
A precise number and a very short sentence: we feel Della’s poverty at once.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesTreasuresWhich clues? In which line?
“One was Jim’s gold watch that had been his father’s and his grandfather’s. The other was Della’s hair.”
The two treasures prepare the twist: each present will be made for the other’s treasure.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandDellaWhat effect? What contrast?
“I had my hair cut off and sold because I couldn’t have lived through Christmas without giving you a present.”
She gives up her treasure for love and buys “a platinum fob chain” for Jim’s watch.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictJimWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: Jim will wear his new chain at once.
Not confirmed: “I sold the watch to get the money to buy your combs.” Each present is now useless: this is situational irony.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningNarratorWhich interpretation do I defend?
“of all who give gifts these two were the wisest.”
Their presents are useless, but their sacrifice proves their love: like the Magi, they give what matters most. The irony becomes tenderness.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in the story (or in the translation). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 4: The Gift of the Magi · Dys-friendly version

Question: Why does the narrator call Della and Jim “the wisest”?

The story

New York, Christmas Eve. Della has one dollar and eighty seven cents to buy a present for her husband Jim. Each of them owns one treasure.

Read the full text of The Gift of the Magi (public domain)

Describe and interpret the picture

Look at the illustration at the top of the page. You can see: a New York avenue in the snow, grey and violet light, carriages, people walking, lights in the windows.

  1. Describe the picture in three sentences.
  2. What does the cold, grey city suggest about Della’s life?
  3. Find one sentence of the text that matches the picture.

Useful phrases: It shows… · In the foreground / background… · The colours suggest… · This reminds me of the moment when… · It reveals that… · I think the artist wants us to feel…

Answer key

A cold, grey city where poor people count every cent; the warm lights are the homes where people wait for Christmas.

“One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all.”
O. Henry, “The Gift of the Magi”, Project Gutenberg #7256

1. Vocabulary

WordMeaningEn français
to saveto keep money for lateréconomiser

2. Characters

CharacterWho?WantsWhat happens

Jimher husbandto buy a perfect present for Dellasells his gold watch
Madame Sofroniehair merchantto buy hairpays twenty dollars

3. The arc of the story

StageIn this story
ExpositionDella has very little money; Christmas is tomorrow.
Inciting incidentShe decides to sell her hair.
Rising actionShe buys a platinum watch chain for Jim.
ClimaxJim comes home and stares at her short hair.
Resolution and twistJim sold his watch to buy combs for her hair.

4. Text dependent questions

  1. How much money does Della have, and how did she save it?
  2. What are the two treasures of the couple?
  3. What does Della buy and why?
  4. Why does Jim stare at Della when he comes in?
  5. Explain the irony of the ending.
  6. Why does the narrator call them “the wisest”?
Answer key
  1. One dollar and eighty seven cents, saved penny by penny by bargaining with the grocer and the butcher.
  2. Jim's gold watch, from his father and grandfather, and Della's long beautiful hair.
  3. A platinum fob chain: it is simple and elegant, worthy of Jim's watch.
  4. He has bought combs for her long hair, which she no longer has.
  5. Each sold their treasure to buy a present for the other's treasure; the gifts are now useless, but their love is proved.
  6. Because their gifts express pure love and sacrifice, like the gifts of the Magi.

5. Speaking

Talk for one minute: what is the most precious thing you own, and would you give it up for someone? Use “I would… because…”.

6. Writing

Write the dialogue between Della and Jim the next morning (8 to 12 lines).

  2. Exercise 2 · Answer: why is the ending ironic?
  3. Exercise 3 · Write 60 words: the best present you ever received, and why.
Answer key: homework
  1. hair · watch · chain · combs
  2. Each sells the treasure the other's present was made for: both presents become useless.
  3. Personal answer; past simple, because, at least three words of the vocabulary.

The story

A winter night in a forest of the eastern Carpathians. Two men, enemies by inheritance, hunt each other. Then a tree falls.

Read the full text of The Interlopers (public domain)

Describe and interpret the picture

Look at the illustration at the top of the page. You can see: a forest of tall dark pines, deep snow, a fallen trunk, grey light, nobody.

  1. Describe the picture in three sentences.
  2. Who are the interlopers in this picture?
  3. Find one sentence of the text that matches the picture.

Useful phrases: It shows… · In the foreground / background… · The colours suggest… · This reminds me of the moment when… · It reveals that… · I think the artist wants us to feel…

Answer key

There are no men: the forest and the snow dominate. Nature is the real intruder in the quarrel.

“Wolves.”
Saki, “The Interlopers”, Project Gutenberg #1477

1. Vocabulary

WordMeaningEn français
feuda long and bitter quarrel between familiesquerelle, vendetta
foresta large area of treesforêt
to poachto hunt illegally on someone's landbraconner
enemya person who hates youennemi
to trapto hold someone so they cannot escapepiéger, coincer
beech treea large tree with smooth grey barkhêtre
to forgiveto stop being angry with someonepardonner
rescuehelp that saves someonesecours
flaska small bottle for alcoholflasque
wolveswild animals like big dogsloups

2. Characters

CharacterWho?WantsWhat happens
Ulrich von Gradwitzowner of the forestto catch his enemytrapped under the tree
Georg Znaeymhis hereditary enemyto hunt on the disputed landtrapped beside Ulrich
The foresterstheir mento find their mastersnever arrive in time

3. The arc of the story

StageIn this story
ExpositionTwo families fight over a strip of forest.
Inciting incidentUlrich and Georg meet face to face in the night.
Rising actionA falling beech tree traps them both.
ClimaxThey become friends and call for help together.
Resolution and twistFigures run towards them: wolves.

4. Text dependent questions

  1. What is the origin of the feud?
  2. Why are the two men in the forest at night?
  3. What happens before they can shoot?
  4. How does their relationship change?
  5. What is the meaning of the title?
  6. Why is the last word so effective?
Answer key
  1. A lawsuit about a narrow strip of forest land, lost by the Znaeym family generations ago.
  2. Ulrich patrols to catch poachers, hoping to meet Georg; Georg is hunting on the disputed land.
  3. A storm brings down a huge beech tree that pins them both to the ground.
  4. Ulrich offers wine from his flask, then friendship; Georg accepts. They plan a future of peace.
  5. Interlopers are intruders: first each man sees the other as one, but the real interlopers are the wolves, or nature itself.
  6. It is a single word that reverses everything: their reconciliation comes too late.

5. Speaking

Debate in groups of four: can a long hatred end in one night? Two for, two against, one minute each.

6. Writing

Write a new ending of 100 words: the foresters arrive first. What happens next?

Homework · required

To do for next lesson. It is checked at the start of the lesson in the Recap check.

  1. Exercise 1 · Gap-fill: The two families have a …… about the forest. A …… tree traps the men. They decide to …… each other. At the end, …… arrive. (feud, beech, forgive, wolves)
  2. Exercise 2 · Answer: who are the real interlopers?
  3. Exercise 3 · Write 60 words: a dialogue between Ulrich and Georg before the wolves come.
Answer key: homework
  1. feud · beech · forgive · wolves
  2. The wolves, or nature: they come between the two men at the very moment of peace.
  3. Model: “Georg, when we get out, come to my house.” “I will, Ulrich. Our fathers were fools.” “Let us be friends now.”

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Edgar Allan Poe, “The Cask of Amontillado” (1846), Project Gutenberg #1063

  • “The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could, but when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge.” (The Cask of Amontillado, opening)
  • “I must not only punish, but punish with impunity.” (The Cask of Amontillado)
  • “The man wore motley. He had on a tight-fitting parti-striped dress, and his head was surmounted by the conical cap and bells.” (The Cask of Amontillado)
  • “My heart grew sick on account of the dampness of the catacombs.” (The Cask of Amontillado)
  • “For the half of a century no mortal has disturbed them. In pace requiescat!” (The Cask of Amontillado, last lines)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeOpeningWhat strikes you first?
“The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could, but when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge.”
A shocking statement, but the “insult” is never explained: we only have Montresor’s word.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesThe planWhich clues? In which line?
“I must not only punish, but punish with impunity.”
Montresor wants a perfect crime: to punish without being punished, and to be known as the avenger by his victim.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandCarnivalWhat effect? What contrast?
“The man wore motley … his head was surmounted by the conical cap and bells.”
Dramatic irony: Fortunato, dressed as a fool, walks into the trap; his name means “fortunate”.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictLast linesWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: Montresor feels no guilt.
Partly confirmed: “My heart grew sick”, but he blames “the dampness of the catacombs”, and he tells the story “For the half of a century” later.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningNarratorWhich interpretation do I defend?
“For the half of a century no mortal has disturbed them. In pace requiescat!”
He never explains the insult, tells the story fifty years later and justifies himself: we cannot fully trust him, and the reader becomes the judge.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in the story (or in the translation). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 6: The Cask of Amontillado · Dys-friendly version

Question: Can we trust Montresor, the narrator of “The Cask of Amontillado”?

Four words:

  • revenge: punishment for a wrong done to you
  • insult: words that hurt someone’s honour
  • carnival: a festival with masks and costumes
  • cask: a large wooden barrel for wine

One line to read: “The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could, but when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge.” (The Cask of Amontillado, opening)

Steps: 1. Read the line aloud. 2. Learn the four words. 3. Do the spiral below, one step at a time. 4. Say your answer with the support sentence.

Lesson 6 · The Cask of Amontillado

Lessons1 · Structure2 · The Necklace3 · Comparative literature4 · The Gift of the Magi5 · The Interlopers6 · The Cask of AmontilladoEvaluationTeacher
Worksheet of this lesson
Scan to open it on a phone or print it.

Recap check · marked · starts as you come in

Sit down, take your notebook and answer on paper at once. 3 students are drawn at random and marked.

  1. What is a feud?
  2. What traps the two men?
  3. What is the last word of the story?
Marking schemePoints
Each correct answer1
Full sentence in Englishbonus 1
Total3 + 1
Answer key
  1. a long quarrel between families
  2. a falling beech tree
  3. Wolves

The story

Carnival in an Italian city. Montresor swears revenge on Fortunato and invites him into his family catacombs to taste a rare wine. The darkest of our four stories.

Read the full text of The Cask of Amontillado (public domain)

Describe and interpret the picture

Look at the illustration at the top of the page. You can see: a vault with stalactites and bricks, a man in a patterned costume chained to the wall, a jester’s cap on the floor, a face looking over the wall.

  1. Describe the picture in three sentences.
  2. What elements create Poe's dark effect? Which detail is ironic?
  3. Find one sentence of the text that matches the picture.

Useful phrases: It shows… · In the foreground / background… · The colours suggest… · This reminds me of the moment when… · It reveals that… · I think the artist wants us to feel…

Answer key

Darkness, the chain, the half-built wall. The jester’s cap is ironic: Fortunato, dressed as a fool, walked into the trap.

“The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could, but when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge.”
Poe, “The Cask of Amontillado”, Project Gutenberg #1063

1. Vocabulary

WordMeaningEn français
revengepunishment for a wrong done to youvengeance
insultwords that hurt someone's honourinsulte
carnivala festival with masks and costumescarnaval
caska large wooden barrel for winetonneau, fût
catacombsunderground tunnels with tombscatacombes
dampslightly wethumide
nichea small space in a wallniche, renfoncement
trowela tool to spread mortartruelle
to chainto attach with metal linksenchaîner
unreliable narratora storyteller we cannot fully trustnarrateur non fiable

2. Characters

CharacterWho?WantsWhat happens
Montresornarrator, a noblemanperfect revenge without punishmentwalls Fortunato in alive
Fortunatoa proud wine expertto taste the Amontilladoburied alive in the vault
Luchesia rival connoisseur, never seennothinga name used as bait

3. The arc of the story

StageIn this story
ExpositionMontresor promises revenge for an insult.
Inciting incidentHe meets Fortunato, drunk, at the carnival.
Rising actionThey descend into the catacombs; Montresor pretends concern.
ClimaxMontresor chains Fortunato in a niche and builds a wall.
Resolution and twistFifty years later, no one has found the bones.

4. Text dependent questions

  1. What does the narrator want, and on what conditions?
  2. How does Montresor lure Fortunato?
  3. Find two examples of irony in Fortunato's costume or name.
  4. Why does Montresor keep suggesting they go back?
  5. Describe the final scene.
  6. Is Montresor a reliable narrator? Justify.
Answer key
  1. Revenge, but he must punish without being punished, and the victim must know who punishes him.
  2. He flatters his pride as a wine expert and mentions a rival, Luchesi, so Fortunato insists on coming.
  3. He wears a jester's costume with bells, a fool going to his death; his name means “fortunate”.
  4. Reverse psychology: it makes Fortunato more determined, and Montresor appears caring.
  5. Montresor chains Fortunato in a niche, builds a wall stone by stone and leaves him in darkness.
  6. No: he never explains the insult, he is telling the story fifty years later and seems to justify himself; his “heart grew sick” may hint at guilt.

5. Speaking

Hot seat: one student is Montresor, fifty years later. The class asks him questions about that night. He must answer in character.

6. Writing

Write Fortunato's point of view in the last minutes (100 to 120 words). Build suspense with short sentences.

Homework · required

To do for next lesson. It is checked at the start of the lesson in the Recap check.

  1. Exercise 1 · Gap-fill: Montresor wants …… . He meets Fortunato during the …… . They go down into the …… . Montresor uses a …… to build the wall. (revenge, carnival, catacombs, trowel)
  2. Exercise 2 · Answer: give two reasons why Montresor is an unreliable narrator.
  3. Exercise 3 · Revise for the evaluation: write ten words from the four vocabulary tables with their meaning.
Answer key: homework
  1. revenge · carnival · catacombs · trowel
  2. He never explains the insult; he tells the story fifty years later to justify himself.
  3. Any ten words of the tables with correct definitions.

If a student cannot attend class or is in hospital

Lesson 6: The Cask of Amontillado. Your lesson at home or in hospital, about 40 minutes, at your own pace. Stop when you are tired: you can do it in two parts.

  1. Read the key lines aloud, slowly, twice:
    • “The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could, but when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge.” (The Cask of Amontillado, opening)
    • “I must not only punish, but punish with impunity.” (The Cask of Amontillado)
    • “The man wore motley. He had on a tight-fitting parti-striped dress, and his head was surmounted by the conical cap and bells.” (The Cask of Amontillado)
    • “My heart grew sick on account of the dampness of the catacombs.” (The Cask of Amontillado)
    • “For the half of a century no mortal has disturbed them. In pace requiescat!” (The Cask of Amontillado, last lines)
  2. Learn the eight words of the Vocabulary box of the lesson: revenge, insult, carnival, cask, catacombs, damp, trowel, unreliable narrator.
  3. Do the spirale de Gorse: copy the five steps on your worksheet (or use the worksheet of this lesson). For each step, write one idea and one line from the text. Then check below.
  4. Quick check: Complete with: revenge, insult, carnival, cask, catacombs, damp, trowel, unreliable narrator.
    • Montresor wants ______.
    • He says Fortunato made an ______.
    • They meet during the ______.
    • Fortunato wants to taste the wine in the ______.
    • They go down into the ______.
    • The walls are cold and ______.
    • Montresor uses a ______ to build the wall.
    • We cannot trust Montresor: he is an ______.
  5. Send to your teacher through the school’s online messaging: read the opening and the last lines. Answer in 100 words: can we trust Montresor? Give two reasons and use must have, may have and can’t have.
Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (Opening): “The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could, but when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge.” A shocking statement, but the “insult” is never explained: we only have Montresor’s word.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (The plan): “I must not only punish, but punish with impunity.” Montresor wants a perfect crime: to punish without being punished, and to be known as the avenger by his victim.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Carnival): “The man wore motley … his head was surmounted by the conical cap and bells.” Dramatic irony: Fortunato, dressed as a fool, walks into the trap; his name means “fortunate”.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (Last lines): Hypothesis: Montresor feels no guilt. Partly confirmed: “My heart grew sick”, but he blames “the dampness of the catacombs”, and he tells the story “For the half of a century” later.
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (Narrator): “For the half of a century no mortal has disturbed them. In pace requiescat!” He never explains the insult, tells the story fifty years later and justifies himself: we cannot fully trust him, and the reader becomes the judge.
Check my quick check
  1. revenge
  2. insult
  3. carnival
  4. cask
  5. catacombs
  6. damp
  7. trowel
  8. unreliable narrator

Evaluation · out of 20

Length: 55 minutes. Read the extract (end of “The Cask of Amontillado”, Poe, 1846, public domain), then answer.

"Fortunato!" No answer. I called again-- "Fortunato--" No answer still. I thrust a torch through the remaining aperture and let it fall within. There came forth in reply only a jingling of the bells. My heart grew sick on account of the dampness of the catacombs. I hastened to make an end of my labour. I forced the last stone into its position; I plastered it up. Against the new masonry I re-erected the old rampart of bones. For the half of a century no mortal has disturbed them. In pace requiescat!

Part A · Comprehension (10 points)

  1. 1. Who is speaking and to whom, in the last lines? (2 pts)
  2. 2. Find two words that create a dark atmosphere. (2 pts)
  3. 3. Find the sentence that suggests Montresor may feel guilt, and say how he explains it. (3 pts)
  4. 4. How much time has passed since that night? Why is it important? (3 pts)

Part B · Vocabulary of the sequence (4 points)

  1. 5. Give the English word: a long quarrel between families (The Interlopers). (1 pt)
  2. 6. A large barrel for wine. (1 pt)
  3. 7. Money you owe (The Necklace). (1 pt)
  4. 8. When the result is the opposite of what we expect. (1 pt)

Part C · Writing (6 points)

Write a short story of 150 to 200 words with a hook and a twist ending. Title: “The Last Gift”.

Marking scheme

PartPoints
A · Comprehension10
B · Vocabulary4
C · Writing6
Total20
Answer key
  1. Montresor, the narrator, tells the story to an unnamed listener who “knows his soul”; Fortunato is dying behind the wall.
  2. For example: catacombs, bones, darkness, damp, niche.
  3. “My heart grew sick”: he says it is because of the damp of the catacombs.
  4. Half a century, fifty years: he was never punished, which fulfils his plan.
  5. feud
  6. cask
  7. debt
  8. irony

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 1: How a short story works

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: The opening lines of the four stories of the sequence, with the story arc and the types of hook and ending

  • “The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could, but when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge.” (Poe, The Cask of Amontillado, 1846)
  • “One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all.” (O. Henry, The Gift of the Magi, 1905)
  • “The girl was one of those pretty and charming young creatures who sometimes are born, as if by a slip of fate, into a family of clerks.” (Maupassant, The Necklace, 1884, transl. Project Gutenberg #3090)
  • “A short story can be read in one sitting. Edgar Allan Poe, one of the inventors of the genre, wanted every word to serve a single effect.” (Lesson document)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticePoeWhat strikes you first?
“A short story can be read in one sitting”; Poe “wanted every word to serve a single effect” (lesson document).
Few characters, one main event: everything in a short story leads to one effect, very often a final surprise.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesOpeningsWhich clues? In which line?
“One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all.” (O. Henry); “I vowed revenge.” (Poe); “as if by a slip of fate, into a family of clerks” (Maupassant).
A precise detail, a shocking statement and a portrait: each first line raises a question that the reader wants answered.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandArcWhat effect? What contrast?
Exposition, inciting incident, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution (story arc table).
Tension grows up to a turning point; in our four stories, the resolution hides a twist.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictEndingsWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: every short story ends with a happy surprise.
Not confirmed: a twist can be bitter (situational irony in The Necklace), tender (The Gift of the Magi) or terrible (“Wolves.” in The Interlopers); an ending can also be open or moral (endings table).
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningAllWhich interpretation do I defend?
“when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge” (Poe) and “That was all.” (O. Henry).
A short story is built from its last line backwards: a hook to catch us, rising tension, and a twist that makes us reread the story differently.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in the story (or in the translation). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 1: How a short story works · Dys-friendly version

Question: How is a short story built, from its first line to its last surprise?

Four words:

  • exposition: the beginning: who, where, when
  • inciting incident: the event that starts the problem
  • rising action: the part where tension grows
  • climax: the turning point of the story

One line to read: “The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could, but when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge.” (Poe, The Cask of Amontillado, 1846)

Objective

Understand how a short story is built, from its first line to its last surprise. Final task of the sequence: write the opening and the twist of your own short story.

What is a short story?

A short story can be read in one sitting. Edgar Allan Poe, one of the inventors of the genre, wanted every word to serve a single effect. Few characters, one main event, and very often a final surprise.

1. The story arc

StageQuestion to askKey words
ExpositionWho? Where? When?setting, characters
Inciting incidentWhat starts the problem?suddenly, one day
Rising actionHow does tension grow?then, as, while
ClimaxWhat is the turning point?at that moment
Falling actionWhat are the consequences?after that
ResolutionHow does it end?finally, in the end

2. Hooking the reader

Type of hookHow it worksOur stories
In medias resthe story starts in the middle of the actionThe Interlopers
A shocking statementthe narrator confesses something strongThe Cask of Amontillado
A precise detaila number or object raises a questionThe Gift of the Magi
A portraita character and her desireThe Necklace

Worksheet: match each opening with a type of hook

Opening lineType of hook
“The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could, but when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge.”...
“One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all.”...
“The girl was one of those pretty and charming young creatures who sometimes are born, as if by a slip of fate, into a family of clerks.”...
Answer key
  • The Cask of Amontillado: A shocking statement
  • The Gift of the Magi: A precise detail
  • The Necklace: A portrait

3. Twist endings

Type of endingDefinitionEffect on the reader
Twist endingan unexpected final revelationsurprise, we reread the story differently
Situational ironythe result is the opposite of what the characters expectbitterness or tenderness
Open endingthe reader must imagine what comes nextsuspense, discussion
Moral endingthe narrator gives a lessonreflection

Speaking

In pairs, tell the ending of a film or series that surprised you. Your partner names the type of ending.

Writing

Write the first sentence of a story using one type of hook (one or two sentences).

C1/C2 track

Read the definition of the short story by Poe in his review of Hawthorne (1842): the writer conceives “a certain unique or single effect”. In 150 words, explain why a twist ending suits this idea, and when it can feel artificial.

Homework · required

To do for next lesson. It is checked at the start of the lesson in the Recap check.

  1. Exercise 1 · Put the stages of the arc in order: climax, exposition, resolution, rising action, inciting incident, falling action.
  2. Exercise 2 · Match: (a) In medias res (b) A shocking statement (c) A precise detail. 1. “One dollar and eighty-seven cents.” 2. The story starts in the middle of the action. 3. “I vowed revenge.”
  3. Exercise 3 · Write the first two sentences of a story with a hook (30 words).
Answer key: homework
  1. exposition, inciting incident, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution
  2. a2, b3, c1
  3. Model: “The letter had been waiting under the door for ten years. Nobody in the house dared to open it.”

For the teacher

If a student cannot attend class or is in hospital

Lesson 1: How a short story works. Your lesson at home or in hospital, about 40 minutes, at your own pace. Stop when you are tired: you can do it in two parts.

  1. Read the key lines aloud, slowly, twice:
    • “The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could, but when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge.” (Poe, The Cask of Amontillado, 1846)
    • “One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all.” (O. Henry, The Gift of the Magi, 1905)
    • “The girl was one of those pretty and charming young creatures who sometimes are born, as if by a slip of fate, into a family of clerks.” (Maupassant, The Necklace, 1884, transl. Project Gutenberg #3090)
    • “A short story can be read in one sitting. Edgar Allan Poe, one of the inventors of the genre, wanted every word to serve a single effect.” (Lesson document)
  2. Learn the eight words of the Vocabulary box of the lesson: exposition, inciting incident, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution, hook, twist.
  3. Do the spirale de Gorse: copy the five steps on your worksheet (or use the worksheet of this lesson). For each step, write one idea and one line from the text. Then check below.
  4. Quick check: Complete with: exposition, inciting incident, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution, hook, twist.
    • The ______ tells us who, where and when.
    • The invitation to a ball is the ______ of The Necklace.
    • During the ______, tension grows.
    • The ______ is the turning point.
    • The ______ shows the consequences.
    • The ______ is how the story ends.
    • A good ______ catches the reader in the first line.
    • A ______ makes us reread the whole story.
  5. Send to your teacher through the school’s online messaging: copy the six steps of the story arc. Then tell the plot of a film or series you know in six sentences, one per step, with one, suddenly, then, at that moment, after that, finally.
Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (Poe): “A short story can be read in one sitting”; Poe “wanted every word to serve a single effect” (lesson document). Few characters, one main event: everything in a short story leads to one effect, very often a final surprise.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (Openings): “One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all.” (O. Henry); “I vowed revenge.” (Poe); “as if by a slip of fate, into a family of clerks” (Maupassant). A precise detail, a shocking statement and a portrait: each first line raises a question that the reader wants answered.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Arc): Exposition, inciting incident, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution (story arc table). Tension grows up to a turning point; in our four stories, the resolution hides a twist.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (Endings): Hypothesis: every short story ends with a happy surprise. Not confirmed: a twist can be bitter (situational irony in The Necklace), tender (The Gift of the Magi) or terrible (“Wolves.” in The Interlopers); an ending can also be open or moral (endings table).
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (All): “when he ventured upon insult I vowed revenge” (Poe) and “That was all.” (O. Henry). A short story is built from its last line backwards: a hook to catch us, rising tension, and a twist that makes us reread the story differently.
Check my quick check
  1. exposition
  2. inciting incident
  3. rising action
  4. climax
  5. falling action
  6. resolution
  7. hook
  8. twist

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 2: The Necklace

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Guy de Maupassant, “The Necklace” (La Parure, 1884), English translation, Project Gutenberg #3090

  • “She had no gowns, no jewels, nothing. And she loved nothing but that. She felt made for that.” (The Necklace, opening)
  • “This life lasted ten years.” (The Necklace)
  • “She had become the woman of impoverished households, strong and hard and rough.” (The Necklace)
  • ““Oh, my poor Mathilde! Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!”” (The Necklace, last line)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeOpeningWhat strikes you first?
“She had no gowns, no jewels, nothing. And she loved nothing but that. She felt made for that.”
The negations and “made for that” show the gap between her dream and her real life as the wife of a clerk.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesThe lossWhich clues? In which line?
To replace the lost necklace, Loisel goes “laying upon the jeweler's counter thirty-six thousand francs.”
Instead of telling the truth, the couple buys a copy: pride turns a loss into a huge debt.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandTen yearsWhat effect? What contrast?
“This life lasted ten years.” and “strong and hard and rough”.
One short sentence alone in its paragraph sums up ten years; the repeated “and” shows the weight of the work.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictLast lineWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: the sacrifice was useful, because the Loisels replaced a real diamond necklace.
Not confirmed: “Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!” The twist turns ten years of work into bitter irony.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningNarratorWhich interpretation do I defend?
“How strange and changeful is life! How small a thing is needed to make or ruin us!”
A small thing ruins her, but pride and appearances are responsible too: she borrowed to look rich and never dared to tell the truth.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in the story (or in the translation). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 2: The Necklace · Dys-friendly version

Question: Why does a borrowed necklace cost Mathilde ten years of her life?

The story

Paris, the 1880s. Mathilde Loisel, married to a modest clerk, dreams of luxury. An invitation to a ball and a borrowed necklace change her life for ten long years.

Read the full text of The Necklace (public domain)

From La Parure to The Necklace

You already know this story from French class. In the next lesson, Comparative literature, you will put the French and English texts side by side.

Describe and interpret the picture

Look at the illustration at the top of the page. You can see: a young woman in a pink ball gown, a fan, men in black evening dress, a crowded salon, chandeliers.

  1. Describe the picture in three sentences.
  2. Which moment of the story could it show? What does her face suggest about her desire to be admired?
  3. Find one sentence of the text that matches the picture.

Useful phrases: It shows… · In the foreground / background… · The colours suggest… · This reminds me of the moment when… · It reveals that… · I think the artist wants us to feel…

Answer key

The ball at the Ministry: Mathilde is the prettiest woman there and every man looks at her. Her triumph is the life she believes she deserves.

“She had no gowns, no jewels, nothing. And she loved nothing but that. She felt made for that.”
Maupassant, “The Diamond Necklace”, transl. Project Gutenberg #3090

1. Vocabulary

WordMeaningEn français
dowrymoney a bride brings to her marriagedot
clerkan office worker in a ministrycommis, employé
to borrowto take something you will give backemprunter
ballan elegant evening party with dancingbal
jewela precious stone or ornamentbijou
to replaceto put a new thing instead of a lost oneremplacer
debtmoney you owedette
to sacrificeto give up something precioussacrifier
pridea strong sense of your own dignityfierté, orgueil
pasteimitation stones made of glassstrass, faux

2. Characters

CharacterWho?WantsWhat happens
Mathilde Loiselyoung wife of a clerkluxury, admirationten years of hard work, poverty
Monsieur Loiselher husband, a modest clerkto make her happysacrifices his savings and his youth
Madame Forestiera rich school friendto help Mathildelearns the truth at the end

3. The arc of the story

StageIn this story
ExpositionMathilde is unhappy with her modest life.
Inciting incidentThe invitation to the Minister's ball.
Rising actionThe dress, the borrowed necklace, the triumph at the ball.
ClimaxThe necklace is lost.
Falling actionTen years of debt and work.
Resolution and twistThe necklace was paste, worth five hundred francs.

4. Text dependent questions

  1. Why is Mathilde unhappy at the start of the story?
  2. How does her husband react to her tears about the dress?
  3. What does Mathilde choose at Madame Forestier's, and why?
  4. What do the Loisels decide when the necklace is lost?
  5. How does Mathilde change during the ten years?
  6. Explain the twist ending.
Answer key
  1. She feels born for luxury but lives in a modest home with a clerk; she suffers from the gap between her dreams and her reality.
  2. He gives her the four hundred francs he saved for a gun, which shows his love and his sacrifice.
  3. A diamond necklace: it is the most dazzling jewel, it matches her dream of elegance.
  4. They buy a similar necklace for thirty six thousand francs and return it without telling the truth.
  5. She becomes strong, rough and poor; she does the heavy housework and bargains at the market.
  6. Madame Forestier reveals that the necklace was imitation, worth at most five hundred francs: ten years were sacrificed for nothing.

5. Speaking

Role play in pairs: Mathilde meets Madame Forestier ten years later. One student is Mathilde, the other her friend. Two minutes, then switch.

6. Writing

Write Mathilde's diary entry on the night of the ball (80 to 120 words). Use the past simple and at least four words from the vocabulary table.

C1/C2 track

Is “The Necklace” a moral tale or an ironic one? Discuss in 250 words, analysing the role of pride, appearance and social class. Compare with a modern form of “keeping up appearances” such as social media.

Homework · required

To do for next lesson. It is checked at the start of the lesson in the Recap check.

  1. Exercise 1 · Gap-fill: Mathilde …… a necklace from her friend. She …… it after the ball. The Loisels pay their …… for ten years. In the end, the necklace was …… . (borrows, loses, debt, paste)
  2. Exercise 2 · True or false? Justify. a) Monsieur Loisel is rich. b) Mathilde chooses a diamond necklace. c) Madame Forestier knows the truth at the start.
  3. Exercise 3 · Answer in 50 words: is Mathilde a victim or responsible for her fate?
Answer key: homework
  1. borrows · loses · debt · paste
  2. a) False, he is a modest clerk. b) True. c) False, she learns at the end that they replaced it.
  3. Model: Mathilde is partly a victim of her social class, but her pride is responsible: she borrows a jewel to appear rich and never dares to tell the truth, which costs her ten years.

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 3: Comparative literature: La Parure and The Necklace

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Guy de Maupassant, « La Parure » (Contes du jour et de la nuit, 1885, Wikisource) and its English translation (Project Gutenberg #3090), side by side

  • “« C’était une de ces jolies et charmantes filles, nées, comme par une erreur du destin, dans une famille d’employés. » / “as if by a slip of fate, into a family of clerks.”” (La Parure / The Necklace, opening)
  • “« Elle n’avait pas de toilettes, pas de bijoux, rien. » / “She had no gowns, no jewels, nothing.”” (La Parure / The Necklace)
  • “« Et cette vie dura dix ans. » / “This life lasted ten years.”” (La Parure / The Necklace)
  • “« Mais la mienne était fausse. Elle valait au plus cinq cents francs !… » / “Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!”” (La Parure / The Necklace, last line)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeOpeningWhat strikes you first?
« comme par une erreur du destin » becomes “as if by a slip of fate”.
“Slip” is lighter than « erreur »: fate looks accidental, and the narrator’s irony is kept.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesWordsWhich clues? In which line?
« Elle n’avait pas de toilettes » becomes “She had no gowns”.
« toilettes » is a false friend: the translator chooses “gowns”, elegant dresses, not toilets.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandRhythmWhat effect? What contrast?
« Et cette vie dura dix ans. » (6 words) / “This life lasted ten years.” (5 words), each alone in its paragraph.
The rhythm is kept: one short sentence stops the reader and sums up ten years.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictLast lineWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: the twist is exactly the same in English.
Partly confirmed: “paste” keeps the surprise, but « fausse » is clearer, and « !… » leaves a silence that the English “!” loses. The double meaning of « La Parure » (a set of jewels, and finery) is lost in the title.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningBothWhich interpretation do I defend?
“as if by a slip of fate” and “Why, my necklace was paste!”
A translation keeps the story, the irony and the rhythm, but it loses sounds and double meanings: reading both texts shows the choices behind every word.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in the story (or in the translation). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 3: Comparative literature: La Parure and The Necklace · Dys-friendly version

Question: What does a translation keep, lose and gain?

Four words:

  • original: the text as the author wrote it
  • translation: the text rewritten in another language
  • translator: the person who translates
  • false friend: a word that looks the same but means something else

One line to read: “« C’était une de ces jolies et charmantes filles, nées, comme par une erreur du destin, dans une famille d’employés. »” (La Parure / The Necklace, opening)

Steps: 1. Read the line aloud. 2. Learn the four words. 3. Do the spiral below, one step at a time. 4. Say your answer with the support sentence.

  • “« Elle n’avait pas de toilettes, pas de bijoux, rien. » / “She had no gowns, no jewels, nothing.”” (La Parure / The Necklace)
  • “« Et cette vie dura dix ans. » / “This life lasted ten years.”” (La Parure / The Necklace)
  • “« Mais la mienne était fausse. Elle valait au plus cinq cents francs !… » / “Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!”” (La Parure / The Necklace, last line)

The rhythm is kept.

Almost: the silence is lost.

Same story, other choices.
